title: Chapter 39. Of the Signification in Scripture of the Word Church
paragraphs: The word 'Church' (Ecclesia) signifies several different things in the books of Holy Scripture. Sometimes—though not often—it is used for God's house, meaning a temple in which Christians assemble to carry out holy duties in public, as in 1 Cor. 14:34: 'Let your women keep silent in the churches.' This use is metaphorical: the word first stood for the congregation assembled there, and only later came to be used for the building itself, to distinguish the temples of Christians from those of idolaters. The temple of Jerusalem was God's house, and the house of prayer; and so is any building Christians dedicate to the worship of Christ, Christ's house. That is why the Greek fathers call it Kuriake, the Lord's house; and from that, in our language, it came to be called Kyrke, and Church.

Church (when it does not mean a building) signifies the same thing Ecclesia signified in the Greek commonwealths: a congregation, or an assembly of citizens, called together to hear the magistrate speak to them. The Roman commonwealth called this same kind of assembly Concio, and the speaker was called Ecclesiastes, and Concionator. When they were called together by lawful authority (Acts 19:39), it was, in Latin, Ecclesia Legitima, and in Greek, Ennomos Ecclesia — both meaning simply "a lawful church." But when they were stirred up by disorderly and seditious clamor, it was what the Greeks called Ecclesia Sugkechumene — "a confused church."

It is also used sometimes for those who have the right to belong to the congregation, though not actually assembled—that is, for the whole multitude of Christian people, however widely scattered: as in Acts 8:3, where it says that 'Saul made havoc of the church.' And in this sense Christ is said to be head of the church. Sometimes it is used for a particular group of Christians, as in Col. 4:15: 'Greet the church that is in his house.' Sometimes, too, it means only the elect, as in Eph. 5:27: 'A glorious church, without spot, or wrinkle, holy, and without blemish'—meaning what Hobbes calls the "church triumphant," or — in other words — the church still to come: the church in its final, glorified state. Sometimes it means a congregation assembled of professing Christians, whether their profession is genuine or false, as is meant in Matt. 18:17, where it says, 'Tell it to the church, and if he fails to hear the church, let him be to you as a Gentile, or a tax collector.'

And it is only in this last sense that the church can be treated as one person—that is, can be said to have the power to will, to declare, to command, to be obeyed, to make laws, or to do any other action whatsoever. For without authority from a lawful congregation, whatever act is done in a gathering of people is only the individual act of each person present who took part in it. It is not the act of all of them together, as one body. And it is certainly not the act of anyone who was absent, or who was present but unwilling for it to be done. In this sense, I define a CHURCH to be, 'a company of men professing the Christian religion, united in the person of one sovereign, at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.' (Here "person" is used in its political sense: a single sovereign authority, not necessarily one individual ruler.) And because in every commonwealth an assembly held without warrant from the civil sovereign is unlawful, a church too, assembled in any commonwealth that has forbidden it to assemble, is an unlawful assembly.

It follows too that there is no such universal church on earth that all Christians are bound to obey, because there is no power on earth to which all other commonwealths are subject. There are Christians in the territories of various princes and states; but each of them is subject to the commonwealth of which he is himself a member, and consequently cannot be subject to the commands of any other person. And therefore a church, of the kind capable of commanding, judging, absolving, condemning, or doing any other such act, is the same thing as a civil commonwealth made up of Christian men, and is called a civil state because its subjects are men, and a church because its subjects are Christians. 'Temporal' and 'spiritual' government are only two words brought into the world to make men see double, and mistake who their lawful sovereign is. It is true that after the resurrection the bodies of the faithful will be not only spiritual but eternal; but in this life they are material, and corruptible. There is therefore no other government in this life, neither of state nor of religion, but temporal government. And no subject may lawfully teach any doctrine that the governor — who governs both state and religion — forbids to be taught. And that governor must be one, or else faction and civil war must inevitably follow in the commonwealth—between church and state, between those who claim spiritual authority and those who claim temporal authority, between the sword of justice and the shield of faith; and (what is more) in every Christian man's own breast — between the Christian and the man. The teachers of the church are called pastors — and so are civil sovereigns. But if pastors are not subordinate one to another, so that there may be one chief pastor, men will be taught contrary doctrines, of which both could be false, and at least one must be false. Who that one chief pastor is, according to the law of nature, has already been shown—namely, that it is the civil sovereign. And to whom Scripture has assigned that office, we shall see in the chapters that follow.
